doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Trumpet recordings every student should hear
summary: He recommends Clifford Brown with Strings, early 60s Miles, and Dizzy and Parker records, again noting the blues is missing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you had to make a short list of trumpet players that every aspiring student should listen to, and really listen to, who would they be?

Okay. My first thing is whenever someone comes to me and says they want to study jazz, they want to try to play jazz trumpet, the first thing I tell them is go out and buy “Clifford © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Brown with Strings,” and I’m going to give you a free lesson. That’s always my deal. Because Clifford Brown displayed, on that CD, record, tape, whatever you have of it, how to play melody. Every song on there is a ballad. And Neal Hefti wrote some unbelievable string parts on there. And Clifford Brown just played the trumpet the way it’s supposed to be played. I mean he’s breathing, his accents, and just he knew when to swell a note or when to be really quiet. And you know like when he did “Embraceable You,” just the first note on that [scats], the way he played that note, is like — I mean you have to listen to it, you know what I mean. People say oh yeah, yeah, well okay. But you’re not listening if you think of it like that. That attack on that first note is that big man. It’s just like he didn’t sneak up on that sucker man. And I would think some of that early 60s Miles Davis, just about anything from Miles. “Seven Steps to Heaven,” “Milestones,” all of that stuff. Because that’s when Miles was playing man. He really was redefining jazz. And that modal thing was just working into him. Because he had influenced musicians that he’d hired, and then they kind of influenced him, you know how that kind of went. I mean quite naturally any Dizzy Gillespie/Charlie Parker record, boy ‘cause those guys, like “Groovin’ High,” the arrangements [scats]. And that was so defining of, hey man something is really about to happen here. And it’s just kind of like prelude to Bebop. I mean it’s just like, and in some ways the introduction was more complex than the tune itself. You know? Like some of those, like on “Salt Peanuts,” [scats] man that’s some bad stuff man. And it’s like but still there’s an element of blues there man. The blues is just waving at you the whole while man. And a lot of the contemporary music, I don’t, I mean the blues is just like hiding in the corner somewhere. You know guys will bend a note every now and then, but it just seems like they’re physically bending it, not emotionally bending it. And I don’t know what that’s from. I don’t know where it went. But we’ve got people who would claim that they’re really playing the blues and if that’s written somewhere, the pen is more powerful than the voice or the sword or anything else. So if it’s written somewhere, this guy must be doing it.
